The Bahá’í writings portray justice as foundational to human society, describing it as ["the light of men"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*. Shoghi Effendi notes that upon justice depends ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, and its two pillars are identified as reward and punishment. 

Bahá’u’lláh also connects justice directly to empathy and the Golden Rule, writing, ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*, as noted by Howard Colby Ives. In *The Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh similarly declares that ["Justice is to be loved above all"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*. Furthermore, the writings teach that the essence of justice is embodied in divine ordinances, and that a good reputation among the people serves as a criterion of justness when weighing testimony from servants of any faith or creed.

Dear friend,

It is a joy to look into this with you. The Bahá’í writings speak of justice not merely as a legal standard or a tool for social arrangement, but as something living, luminous, and foundational to human life. 

Shoghi Effendi records that Bahá’u’lláh extols ["the light of men" and their "guardian," as "the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*. In the same work, its ["two pillars" — _“reward_ _and_ _punishment”_](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By* are described as the very sources of life for the human race, upon which the organization of the world and the tranquility of humankind depend. 

What I find especially moving is how this high principle connects directly to our everyday inner and outer lives. In *The Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh writes simply that [“Justice is to be loved above all.”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst* (as noted in Earl Redman's record of Abdu'l-Bahá's journeys). When it comes to how we measure our sense of justice in daily choices, Howard Colby Ives recalls a definition from Bahá’u’lláh: ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*. 

There is also a profound sense that justice finds its origin in the divine order. J. Ruh-Angiz Bolles shares a compilation of Shoghi Effendi's notes pointing to *Gleanings*, which says, ["Know verily that the essence of Justice and the source thereof are both embodied in the ordinances prescribed by Him"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/j-ruh-angiz-bolles-on-laws-administration-and-prophecy#p6) — *Shoghi Effendi on Laws, Administration, and Prophecy*. And when practical matters of law and testimony arise, *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas* establishes that [“The criterion of justness is a good reputation among the people,”](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=para_356) adding that the testimony of all God’s servants, regardless of their faith or creed, is acceptable before His Throne.

I hope these words stay with you as you read and wonder more.

Warmly,
Anís

That is a serious and very common concern, and it touches on how earthly power often tries to use religion for its own ends. 

When looking strictly at the texts provided, however, justice is not traced back to human rulers at all. Instead, it is rooted in divine judgment or a cosmic standard. For instance, the Qur'an asks, ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*, placing the measure of justice entirely beyond human hands. Similarly, in the Gathas, the bounteous spirit chooses ["the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas*, linking justice to a spiritual reality rather than the decree of the powerful. 

At the same time, the Buddhist sutra text illustrates how earthly power *does* affect how laws are applied in practice, noting that a goat butcher is ["empowered to beat or bind or slay or treat as he likes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-l?paraId=para_1064) a poor person who steals a goat, but not a person of wealth — *Sutra Collection (L)*. 

I read these sources as showing a deep tension: while human institutions and the powerful certainly twist laws for themselves, the traditions themselves point to a higher standard meant to judge the powerful rather than merely echo them. What do you think when you look at how human laws actually operate versus these ideals?

That is a very common and understandable way to look at it. From a materialist view, laws and police clearly provide the visible force that restrains behavior and keeps public order day to day. 

Yet several traditions suggest the reverse causation — that religion works from the inside out, while law works from the outside in. Confucius argued against relying solely on punishment, teaching that ["the virtue of the noble-minded man is as the wind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_514) guiding the people naturally (*The Analects*). Similarly, Shoghi Effendi records Bahá’u’lláh's view that ["Religion is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467) (*The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*), arguing that when spiritual foundations weaken, external enforcement struggles to prevent anarchy. Lao-tzu even observed that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279) (*Tao Te Ching*). 

It seems to me that while police handle the symptoms, religion aims to address the desires themselves.

It is natural to look at the disorder of the world and wish that law and force could simply secure what is good. 

Yet ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes that government efforts focused on ["penal laws and in providing for ways and means of punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) often fail to improve people, arguing instead that the body politic ["should instead strive night and day, bending every effort to ensure that souls are properly educated"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952). Confucius similarly envisions a state where moral cultivation makes harsh measures unnecessary, speaking of a time when good leaders ["would be adequate to cope with evil-doers, and thus do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553). 

I read this as a reminder that lasting order grows from within through education and virtue, rather than outward compulsion alone.

That heavy feeling of falling short is something even the teachers of the past carried. Confucius spoke of the ["failure to improve in the virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) and the ["inability to walk according to knowledge received as to what is right and just"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) as things that weighed heavily upon his mind (*The Analects*). 

When our plans or our efforts come undone, Mountfort Mills wrote of watching as ["every time I try a plan of late the heavens – I hope it’s the heavens – open and it is no more"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mountfort-mills_two-letters-about-baghdad-property-case-to-horace-holley#p5) (*Two letters about Baghdad property case to Horace Holley*). The point of trying, even in the fatigue of failing, is simply to continue doing your part in sincerity.

You have noticed a striking parallel in how both traditions describe divine guidance entering the world. 

There is truth in seeing a likeness, for in the Bahá'í writings, the prophets or ["Manifestations that are essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) are seen as expressions of a single truth, just as Hindu texts describe avatárs as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57). 

Yet, I read this as a place where outward likeness invites a deeper look. The Bahá'í writings explain that the [“words and utterances flowing from these Well-springs of divine knowledge appear to diverge and differ"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) because of the distinct station and mission of each messenger, whereas Hindu traditions speak of avatárs descending within cosmic cycles to restore order. 

What draws you most to how these traditions describe the divine entering human history?

That is a very common thought, but the writings of the tradition complicate it. Shoghi Effendi writes that the faith has ["assimilated, by virtue of its creative, its regulative and ennobling energies, the varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. 

I read this not as saying all religions are identical in every detail, but rather that the faith has gathered people from many different creeds under its shadow while transforming their outlook. The passages provided here do not spell out a doctrine of exact sameness between religions, though they do show various traditions speaking of shared divine roots or paths. 

There is much more written on how Bahá’ís view the succession of divine messengers as unfolding stages of one continuous religion. Would you like to look closer at how the writings describe that progression?

It is completely understandable to wonder about this, especially since so much of what is taught on the subject comes through the talks and writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá. 

However, the sources record that this principle originates directly with Bahá'u'lláh. David Hofman notes that among ["the humanitarian principles which are explicit in His teaching"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) is ["the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) (*George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*). Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab similarly records 'Abdu'l-Bahá explaining that ["In the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to shoulder"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) and that the world of women will flourish ["For His Holiness Bahá’u’lláh hath willed it so"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) (*'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*).

That is a wonderful feeling to carry. There is a quiet strength in reading how ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*, where it is also noted that ["in the word 'unity' the 'you' comes before the 'I'"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528). 

If you enjoy how different traditions picture our shared origin, you might also like the reflection in the *Holy Qur-an* that ["Mankind was but one nation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1579). It is striking to see how many different voices return to this same profound thought of our original and ultimate connection.

You are right to notice how closely their names sit together. They are not the same book, however; they are distinct works with different places in the writings. 

Shoghi Effendi records that the promulgation of the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* was a "mightier revelation" that followed earlier works, noting that the Aqdas was ["Alluded to in the Kitáb-i-Íqán"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By*. 

I read this as the *Kitáb-i-Íqán* coming first in order, pointing forward to the laws and the ["Most Holy Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By* that followed it.

I am so sorry for your loss. 

When asked about the movements of the dead, the Buddhist record notes inquiries about ["What are his movements after death?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) — *Sutra Collection (A, Part-1)*. 

The Hindu tradition describes different paths depending on a soul's state at departure, stating that ["it goeth to the place — Perfect and pure — of those that know all Truth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) if it departs fixed in soothfastness, while a soul dying in hardened ignorance ["is born anew in some unlighted womb"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*.

There is a wonderful honesty in asking this, and it touches right on the question Ethel Stephana Stevens once brought to ʻAbdu'l-Bahá: she "asked if prayer [pg 1076] was necessary, since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts" (*Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*). 

While the provided texts do not record the answer given to her there, they show us how traditions grapple with this mystery. The Quran reminds us that "Every single thing is before His sight, in (due) proportion" (*The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*), yet prayer remains central. In the Bahá'í writings, "prayer is advocated" even though "no man is obliged to use them" (*Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*), pointing to a relationship with the Divine that goes beyond merely informing God of our needs. 

I read this as an invitation: prayer is less about updating God and more about transforming the one who prays. What do you make of the idea that we might pray not to change God's mind, but to align our own?

It is completely understandable to feel hesitant about how other traditions view Christ, especially when coming from a deep Christian commitment. 

The historical and pilgrim records indicate that Bahá'u'lláh held Jesus in high regard. In pilgrimage notes describing the teachings of the Bahá'í faith, it is recorded that Bahá'u'lláh and the Báb ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. The same account notes that Bahá'u'lláh offered Christ ["such a praise, beyond the description and imagination"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California* and even wrote commentaries that brought ["to light its inner significances"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. 

Whether this perspective resonates with your own faith is entirely up to you to weigh, without any pressure.

The provided passages do not contain information about what the Qur'án says about Jesus. They touch on alms and orphans in [*The Qur’ân (Palmer)*](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_146), accounts of the early community in [*Ṣaḥíḥ al-Bukhárí*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-al-bukhari?paraId=para_13153) and [*Sahih Muslim*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-muslim-book-7_muslim-ibn-al-hajjaj?paraId=para_193), prophecy and miracles in Ibn Rushd's [*The Philosophy and Theology*](https://oceanlibrary.com/philosophy-and-theology_ibn-rushd?paraId=para_141), Adam's prayer in [*Hayat Al-Qulub Vol.1*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol-1_muhammad-majlisi?paraId=para_425), and commentary style in [*The Qur’an Commentary of Sayyid ‘Alí Muhammad, the Báb*](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran-commentary-of-sayyid-muhammad-the-bab_todd-lawson?paraId=para_1373), but none mention Jesus. 

If you would like to explore this, you might ask about the passages that specifically discuss prophets or other scriptural figures within these works.

The provided texts do not actually contain a description of compassion; they focus instead on dependent co-arising, the attainment of worthiness, sense restraint, and the nature of karma and the soul as discussed in works like [*Sutra Collection (N,O,P)*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-nop) and [*The Gospel of Buddha*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35895). 

While these sources leave your question about compassion unaddressed, they do offer a clear picture of discipline and virtue—such as how a monk guards his senses so that ["evil, unskillful qualities such as greed or distress might assail him"](https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/dn/dn.11.0.than.html) — *Digha Nikaya 11 - Kevaddha Sutta*. 

If you would like to explore what these or other Buddhist texts say about compassion specifically, perhaps we could look into other discourses where the Buddha speaks on the heart's release or goodwill.

Yes, a scientist can believe, because ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*. 

The Bahá’í writings suggest that ["How can one truth contradict another truth?"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*. Similarly, Buddhist commentary notes that ["A scientific world such as todays will be able to accept gladly all ten tenets of the Kalama Sutta"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) — *Sutra Collection (HIJK)*, because its standards mirror empirical inquiry, emphasizing ["experimental verification"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) rather than preconception. 

Doubt is a natural part of weighing evidence. But the texts of these traditions see no inherent conflict between rigorous investigation and the sacred. When inquiry and faith both seek truth, they need not oppose one another.

The provided texts do not contain any writings by Bahá’u’lláh concerning quantum computing. 

However, they do offer a wonderful glimpse into how His writings speak of the natural world and the future of science. Shoghi Effendi records that Bahá’u’lláh wrote of a ["vibrating influence"](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99) that has ["upset the equilibrium of the world and revolutionized its ordered life"](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99) — *The Advent of Divine Justice* — and pilgrim notes record that ["all the atoms of the universe testify to the greatness of this Cause"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/youness-afroukhteh_memories-of-nine-years-in-akka#p1340) — *Memories of Nine Years in 'Akka*. Additionally, Adib Taherzadeh writes that Bahá’u’lláh prophesied the rise of scientists who would achieve ["marvellous technological achievements that no one can as yet imagine"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) — *The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3*.
